core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain how Scrooge changes **elsewhere in the novella**. In your answer you must consider: how he is presented at different points; the reasons for the change. You should refer to the context of the novella. (20 marks)

bullets: Thesis: a gradual, emotional transformation from isolation to connection that models the change Dickens wanted in his readers.
P1: Stave 1: cold, isolated, voicing Poor Law and Malthusian attitudes.
P2: Stave 2: memory awakens feeling and regret.
P3: Staves 3–4: empathy for Tiny Tim and fear of death.
P4: Stave 5: generosity and reintegration; purpose.

essays.q: Explain how Scrooge changes elsewhere in the novella.
essays.text:
Dickens presents Scrooge’s transformation as a gradual, emotional journey from isolation to connection, driven by memory, empathy and fear, so that his redemption becomes a model for the change Dickens hoped to provoke in his comfortable Victorian readers.

In Stave 1, Scrooge embodies the attitudes Dickens wanted to attack. He is ‘solitary as an oyster’, and ‘the cold within him’ freezes his features, so his isolation is both physical and moral. When the charity collectors ask for help for the poor, he asks ‘Are there no prisons?’ and ‘the Union workhouses?’, and suggests that the poor should die and ‘decrease the surplus population’. These lines put the logic of the 1834 Poor Law and of Malthus into the mouth of a character the reader dislikes, so that middle-class readers who held these views would hear how heartless they sound. Scrooge insists that the poor are ‘not my business’, a phrase that Marley will soon contradict.

The change begins with memory. The Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge ‘a solitary child, neglected by his friends’, and he weeps. Dickens, who had himself been sent to work in a blacking warehouse at twelve, invites sympathy for the boy without excusing the man: Belle’s accusation that ‘Another idol has displaced me… a golden one’ shows that Scrooge chose money over love. Crucially, memory produces small regrets about the present: he wishes he had given something to a carol singer and spoken kindly to his clerk. Dickens suggests that empathy begins by remembering our own vulnerability.

In Staves 3 and 4, empathy deepens into fear. Watching the Cratchits, Scrooge asks ‘with an interest he had never felt before’ whether Tiny Tim will live, and the Ghost answers with Scrooge’s own words about the ‘surplus population’. The repetition shames him, and Malthus’s abstract theory becomes a named, loved child. Then the silent Phantom of Christmas Yet to Come shows him a death ‘unwatched, unwept, uncared for’, and finally his own name on a neglected grave. Scrooge’s question, whether these are things that ‘Will be’ or ‘May be, only’, reveals his hope, and his vow to ‘honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year’ completes his repentance.

Stave 5 shows the result through deliberate reversal. Scrooge declares himself ‘as light as a feather’, as if freed from Marley’s chains, and he repeats each encounter of Stave 1 with the opposite choice: he gives a large donation with ‘back-payments’ to the charity collector, joins Fred’s party, and raises Bob’s salary, ordering him to ‘Make up the fires’. The tricolon ‘as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man’ shows his reintegration into society, and he becomes ‘a second father’ to Tiny Tim, ‘who did NOT die’. Dickens’s purpose is clear: Scrooge proves that change is possible and joyful, and that it begins with seeing the poor as ‘fellow-passengers to the grave’. The novella’s final hope, that its readers might keep Christmas ‘well’, invites them to make the same journey.
essays.thesis: Dickens presents Scrooge’s transformation as a gradual, emotional journey from isolation to connection, driven by memory, empathy and fear, so that his redemption becomes a model for the change Dickens hoped to provoke in his comfortable Victorian readers.
why: **AO1**: a sustained argument tracking change across all five staves with precise quotations.
**AO3**: Poor Law, Malthus, Dickens’s childhood and purpose, each tied to a moment.
Evaluative ending connecting character and reader.

exam.q: Practice: rewrite P2 using Fezziwig instead of the schoolboy.
exam.tip: Have two pieces of evidence ready for each stave.

mistakes.r: Show the gradual journey across all staves.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on Scrooge’s transformation across the novella, with thesis, plan and notes on how it earns AO1 and AO3 marks.

terms.d: A complete change in character; Scrooge’s is gradual across the staves.
